question: What is a primary responsibility of nurses regarding injection administration?

options.A: Ensuring every injection is given intravenously
options.B: Ensuring every injection is necessary, sterile, and safely disposed of
options.C: Administering injections only when patients explicitly demand them
options.D: Reusing syringes if supplies are limited

explanation: Nurses have the professional duty to verify that injections are truly necessary, prepared with sterile techniques, and disposed of safely to prevent injuries and infections. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h1)

question: Which bloodborne pathogens are specifically highlighted as risks associated with unsafe injections?

options.B: Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV

explanation: Unsafe injection practices primarily transmit bloodborne pathogens like Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h1)

question: What does the 'three-one' approach in safe injection practices refer to?

options.A: One nurse, one patient, one hour
options.B: One needle, one syringe, and one dose used once for a single patient
options.C: One alcohol swab, one plaster, one glove
options.D: One oral drug, one injection, one IV line

explanation: The 'three-one' approach mandates one needle, one syringe, and one administered dose, used only once for a single patient to guarantee safety. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h2)

question: Which of the following represents an unsafe injection practice?

options.A: Disposing of used needles in a puncture-resistant safety box
options.B: Performing hand hygiene before medication preparation
options.C: Recapping used needles using a two-handed technique

explanation: Two-handed recapping significantly increases the risk of accidental needle-stick injuries and is classified as an unsafe practice. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h2)

question: What is a primary health consequence associated with unsafe injections globally?

options.B: Transmission of bloodborne infections such as HIV and viral hepatitis

explanation: Unsafe injections are a major vector for transmitting bloodborne infections like HIV and viral hepatitis globally. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h3)

question: Who, besides the patient receiving the injection, is directly endangered by unsafe disposal of sharps?

options.B: Healthcare workers and community waste handlers

explanation: Healthcare workers face needle-stick risks during administration, while community waste handlers and children face dangers from improperly discarded sharps. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h3)

question: Why do many patients in certain cultural contexts prefer injections over oral medications?

options.A: Injections are always cheaper than pills
options.B: They believe injections work faster and are more potent than oral drugs
options.C: Injections do not require any medical skill to administer
options.D: Oral medications are illegal in most rural clinics

explanation: Cultural beliefs often lead patients to assume that injected medications act faster and possess greater potency than oral alternatives. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h4)

question: What is the most appropriate nursing response to a patient who demands an unnecessary injection?

options.A: Administer the injection immediately to satisfy the patient
options.B: Ignore the patient and walk away
options.C: Provide empathetic, culturally sensitive education on the benefits and safety of oral medications
options.D: Prescribe a higher dose of intravenous fluids instead

explanation: Nurses should use empathetic and culturally sensitive health education to correct misconceptions and explain the safety and effectiveness of oral alternatives. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h4)

question: How do provider knowledge gaps contribute to unnecessary injections?

options.A: Providers may hold outdated beliefs that injections are always medically superior to oral drugs
options.B: Providers forget how to wash their hands properly
options.C: Providers are unaware that needles exist
options.D: Providers only work during night shifts

explanation: Outdated clinical beliefs regarding the superiority of parenteral routes lead providers to prescribe unnecessary injections instead of utilizing effective oral medications. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h5)

question: What intervention helps address provider knowledge gaps regarding rational injection practices?

options.A: Reducing the number of patients in the hospital
options.B: Continuous professional development and regular in-service training
options.C: Banning all medications except intravenous fluids

explanation: Continuous professional development and in-service training help update healthcare providers on evidence-based guidelines and rational prescribing habits. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h5)

question: How do economic factors drive the overuse of injections in certain healthcare settings?

options.A: Injections are always cheaper for the hospital to purchase than pills
options.B: Revenue generation is often linked to the sale of injectable drugs and supplies
options.C: Governments fine hospitals that do not give a minimum number of injections
options.D: Patients refuse to pay for any service that does not involve a syringe

explanation: When revenue generation is tied to commodity sales, providers may recommend unnecessary injections because they are more lucrative than oral medications. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h6)

question: What structural reform can help mitigate financial incentives driving unnecessary injections?

options.A: Separating prescribing from dispensing duties and enforcing transparent pricing
options.B: Eliminating all private healthcare facilities entirely
options.C: Making all injections free of charge without government subsidies
options.D: Requiring patients to buy their own syringes from open markets

explanation: Separating prescribing from dispensing and enforcing pricing transparency reduces the financial motivation for providers to push unnecessary commodities. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h6)

question: What is a dangerous consequence of chronic stockouts of disposable syringes in a facility?

options.A: Patients automatically switch to oral medications
options.B: Staff may resort to unsafe practices like reusing single-use syringes

explanation: Equipment shortages often drive desperate staff to reuse single-use injection equipment, drastically increasing infection risks. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h7)

question: Which systemic failure contributes to improper sharps disposal in healthcare facilities?

options.B: Lack of functional incinerators and secure waste disposal systems
options.C: Too many trained waste management personnel

explanation: A lack of functional incinerators and secure disposal infrastructure leads to improper sharps disposal and community hazards. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h7)

question: What is a potential permanent complication of poorly placed intramuscular injections in pediatric patients?

options.A: Sciatic nerve damage resulting in foot drop

explanation: Poorly placed gluteal injections in children frequently damage the sciatic nerve, leading to permanent motor deficits such as foot drop. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h8)

question: Why do unnecessary injections increase the risk of systemic infections?

options.A: They boost the patient's immune system too rapidly
options.B: They break the skin barrier without valid medical indication, creating portals of entry for pathogens
options.C: They automatically neutralize all antibiotics in the body
options.D: They require patients to stay in the hospital for weeks

explanation: Every skin puncture is a breach in the body's primary defense barrier; performing them unnecessarily increases infection entry points. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h8)

question: What is a key nursing strategy for reducing patient demand for unnecessary injections?

options.A: Scolding patients who ask for injections
options.B: Patient advocacy and education explaining the effectiveness of oral alternatives
options.C: Refusing to give any medications at all
options.D: Charging higher fees for oral drugs

explanation: Educating patients and advocating for them by explaining oral efficacy helps dispel myths and reduces inappropriate injection requests. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h9)

question: Which clinical action is a mandatory part of injection safety protocols for nurses?

options.A: Recapping all needles with both hands before disposal
options.B: Immediately disposing of used sharps into puncture-resistant containers
options.C: Reusing syringes for patients with the same diagnosis
options.D: Skipping hand hygiene to save time during emergencies

explanation: Immediate disposal of sharps into puncture-resistant safety boxes is a fundamental standard precaution preventing needle-stick injuries. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T6#GNS122_U4_T6_h9)
